The proposed solution is incorrect.

To see why, consider the claim that $v(4, \sqrt{2}) = 10$:

We can construct a connected 4-regular graph on $14$ vertices with second largest eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = \sqrt{2}$ from the incidence graph of the unique symmetric $2\text{-}(7, 4, 2)$ design (the complement of the Fano plane):
- Let $B$ be the $7 \times 7$ incidence matrix of the $2\text{-}(7, 4, 2)$ design. Every row and column has degree $k = 4$, and any two distinct blocks intersect in $\lambda = 2$ points.
- Thus, $B B^T = (k - \lambda)I + \lambda J = 2I + 2J$.
- The all-ones matrix $J$ of order 7 has eigenvalues $7$ (multiplicity 1) and $0$ (multiplicity 6). Consequently, $B B^T$ has eigenvalues $2 + 2(7) = 16 = 4^2$ (multiplicity 1) and $2 + 2(0) = 2$ (multiplicity 6).
- The bipartite incidence graph has adjacency matrix $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & B \\ B^T & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ with $14$ vertices.
- The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\pm 4$ (multiplicity 1 each) and $\pm \sqrt{2}$ (multiplicity 6 each).

Since the eigenvalue $4$ has multiplicity 1, this graph is connected, 4-regular, has 14 vertices, and its second largest eigenvalue is precisely $\lambda_2 = \sqrt{2} \le \sqrt{2}$. 

Therefore, $v(4, \sqrt{2}) \ge 14 > 10$, which disproves the value $v(4, \sqrt{2}) = 10$ given in the proposed solution.

VERDICT: REJECT
